scenario: AITA for ignoring my senior associate’s text | Just to give a background story, I’m a first year associate at a local firm and the senior associate in this story has been with the firm for 3 years. So a few weeks ago, I was feeling a little bit under the weather and threw up as soon as I woke up. I notified my senior associate and told her that I won’t be coming to work as I’m not feeling well. She was a bit disappointed but had no choice but to allow me a sick leave. I sent a few emails to our client as per requested by her the previous day and tried to get some sleep. As I’m trying to get some sleep, she kept on texting me with things that I needed to do. I tried to ignore it and turned off my phone’s notification so I can get some sleep. Around an hour later, she called me and told me that I have to sent her a file (regarding client’s data which she doesn’t have on her laptop) immediately as it is an urgent matter. I sent her the files she wanted and asked her if she’ll need anything else as I’m going to the doctor and won’t be bringing my laptop with me. She said that’s all for now. I went to the doctor, and the doctor said I’m overworked (I’ve been working overtime till 2-3AM for the past 2 months) and needs some rest. On my way home, my senior again texted me and told me to get our client’s billing information (something that she could do herself as she also have their contacts). I did as I’m told as fowarded her with the information. I got home, took the prescribed medicine and fell asleep. I was shocked when I woke up to find my phone with 2 miscalled and 30 new messages from her giving me work to do from home. I felt it was a little bit unfair of her to give me work while I’m on a sick leave and so I ignored the message and didn’t reply her. So, AITA for not replying her text? Notes: English is not my first language, I’m sorry if there’s a lot of grammatical errors.

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.
Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently and create a warm, festive atmosphere: ### **1. Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! Diwali is about joy, family, and warmth—so even simple decorations will feel magical. **Shubh Diwali!** 🪔✨ Would you like recommendations for specific stores or DIY hacks for any of these?

Ignoring her was **not about being lazy**—it was about **survival**. - **But**: If you’d **responded minimally** (e.g., *"Not feeling well, will check later"*), you might’ve avoided backlash while still setting a boundary. - **The bigger issue**: **She was wrong to push you while sick**, but **you were also in a vulnerable position** (first-year, no leverage). Ignoring her was a **necessary act of self-care**, but it could’ve been handled more diplomatically. --- ### **What Should You Do Now?** 1. **Reflect on the Long-Term Impact** - If she **reports you for "not responding"**, you can say: *"I was sick and under doctor’s care—I prioritized my health as advised. I’m happy to discuss how to handle urgent matters in the future."* - If she **doesn’t react**, great—you set a boundary. 2. **Protect Your Health** - Follow the doctor’s advice **strictly** (rest, no overtime). If the firm expects this, it’s **their problem**, not yours. - If this happens again, **escalate to a manager** or HR (but do it **calmly**, with examples). 3. **Learn from the Experience** - **Next time you’re sick**: Set **clear expectations upfront** (e.g., *"I’ll check emails once a day but won’t be available for urgent tasks"*). - **Document interactions** (screenshots of texts) in case of future issues. 4. **Consider the Firm Culture** - If this is **normal behavior** at your firm, you might need to **decide if it’s sustainable**. Burnout is real—your health comes first. --- ### **Final Thought:** You were **not wrong for ignoring her**—**you were right to protect your health**. However, **how you handle it moving forward** (communication, escalation) will determine whether this becomes a **positive boundary-setting moment** or a **potential conflict**. Would you like help drafting a **polite but firm reply** to her next time, or advice on how to discuss this with your manager?
